Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
revision_notes: Fetched the cited UNECA Digital Trade Regulatory Integration profile for Namibia; it confirms no data localisation measures are recorded. Cross-checked against DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World guide for Namibia, which states explicitly there are 'no data transfer restrictions in place' and 'no specific laws that regulate the manner in which personal data may be stored or transmitted online', and against a July 2024 Mondaq legal update confirming Namibia's Data Protection Bill (successive 2020/2021/2022/2023 drafts) remains unenacted. Namibia has no comprehensive data protection law and no sectoral or general data localisation requirement in force; the draft Bill, once passed, would regulate cross-border transfer via an adequacy-style test rather than mandate in-country storage. No evidence of financial-sector or critical-infrastructure data residency mandates was found in NAMFISA outsourcing principles or Bank of Namibia payment service determinations reviewed. Score of 1 (No data localisation requirements) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Namibia has not enacted any legal or regulatory requirement mandating that personal, government, financial or critical infrastructure data be stored within national borders. The country lacks comprehensive data protection legislation altogether: successive drafts of a Data Protection Bill (most recently 2023) remain before Parliament and are not yet in force. Sector-specific rules, such as NAMFISA's outsourcing principles for financial institutions and Bank of Namibia payment service determinations, impose confidentiality, security and regulator-access obligations on outsourced data but do not require that data be physically stored inside Namibia. Once enacted, the draft Data Protection Bill would restrict cross-border transfers of personal data to jurisdictions offering an adequate level of protection, but this is a transfer-adequacy mechanism rather than a data localisation mandate.
